Albert Camus was a French writer and thinker born in Algeria, at Mondovi near Annaba, in 1913. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1957.

He grew up poor in a working-class district of Algiers, the son of a pied-noir father killed in the First World War. His novels The Stranger (1942), set in Algiers, and The Plague (1947), set in Oran, made his name. His ideas on the absurd and on revolt were read around the world.

During the Algerian War he called for a truce to spare civilians and refused to back either the FLN or French rule. Both sides attacked him for it. He died in a car crash in France in 1960, two years before independence.
